newsitem.title: GERMANY: German press say Kohl government woes not over yet.
newsitem.headline: German press say Kohl government woes not over yet.

text.p: German press commentators said on Thursday the crisis in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government was far from over after his Finance Minister Theo Waigel survived a parliamentary motion to have him sacked.

Kohl threw his weight on Wednesday behind the beleagured Waigel, struggling to save face after backing off from his grab for Bundesbank gold following strong resistance from the central bank and a threatened revolt by government deputies.
"Kohl protected Waigel in order to protect himself. If Waigel looses authority his boss looses too," wrote the Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung daily in a commentary.

"The coalition survived the parliament debate. But it is by no means over the hump," wrote the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine, adding that despite Kohl's support for Waigel, doubts about his capabilities were spreading in the coalition.
The Handelsblatt business daily, which said on Tuesday the only option left was for Waigel to resign, said the Finance Minister had earned himself one last chance.

"The deep budget problems of the Bonn government remain, but the responsibility for that cannot just be dumped on the Finance Minister. The whole government is guilty of the fact it continues to stand on shaky ground," it wrote, describing the crisis as the most serious yet in Kohl's 15 years as chancellor.
The Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung daily said although the government had won the parliamentary vote it continued to lose the confidence of ordinary people.
"The government has its back to the wall. And nobody seems to be in any position to change that," it wrote.
The Frankfurter Rundschau said Kohl, showing his election-winning prowess, had won an empty victory.

"He is goes from one victory to another but seems not to notice the reality that exists outside parliament," it sneered. "He has not noticed the change in atmosphere outside in the country among those affected by unemployment."
One cartoon pictured the veteran chancellor as a sturdy tree, the word "euro" written on its roots, while another showed Kohl as a stone statue crumbling away at the edges.
The Westdeutsche Allgemeine said Bonn still had to tackle huge budget problems.

"Not a single question has been solved, because everything is still disputed. Taxes up, more borrowing, Bundesbank gold, savings, grabbing for the state's last silverware," it wrote, listing options Bonn is considering to fill a gaping budget hole.
Waigel has suggested further spending cuts and privatisations to raise 19 billion marks ($11 billion) to keep Germany's 1997 budget on target to meet the entry criteria for Europe's single currency.
